query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of Blue

Blue is everywhere now: in jeans, corporate logos, police uniforms, hospital signs, social-media icons, and the imagined color of calm. But for much of human history, blue was rare, difficult to make, and symbolically uncertain.

In the ancient world, blue was not always treated as a major color. Many early languages had no simple word equivalent to modern “blue,” often describing the sea or sky in terms of brightness, darkness, or greenness instead. Yet people still valued blue materials when they could get them. In ancient Egypt, blue became especially important. Egyptians associated it with the Nile, the heavens, rebirth, and divine protection. They developed one of the earliest synthetic pigments, Egyptian blue, made from silica, lime, copper, and alkali, and used it in tombs, statues, and decoration.

For centuries, one of the most prized blue substances was lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone mined mainly in what is now Afghanistan. Ground into pigment, it became ultramarine — literally “from beyond the sea,” because it reached Europe through long trade routes. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, ultramarine was more expensive than many other pigments, sometimes even rivaling gold. Artists reserved it for the most sacred or prestigious subjects, especially the robes of the Virgin Mary. Blue therefore became linked with holiness, purity, and spiritual depth.

But blue’s rise was gradual. In ancient Rome, it could be associated with foreigners, barbarians, or mourning. Red, white, black, and gold often carried more prestige. By the later Middle Ages, however, blue gained status in Europe. French kings adopted blue decorated with golden fleurs-de-lis, and stained-glass windows filled cathedrals with luminous cobalt light. The color moved from the margins toward the center of power.

The story changed again with trade, chemistry, and industry. Indigo dye, derived from plants, had long been used in Asia, Africa, and the Americas. As global trade expanded, indigo became one of the major commodities of empire, cultivated through colonial systems and enslaved labor. Its rich, durable color transformed textiles, uniforms, and everyday clothing. Later, synthetic dyes made blue far cheaper and more widely available.

In the eighteenth century, a new pigment, Prussian blue, was discovered accidentally in Berlin. It was strong, affordable, and reliable, and it quickly spread through painting, printing, and decoration. Other synthetic blues followed. By the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, blue had become a color of mass culture: naval uniforms, workwear, school uniforms, denim, and eventually blue jeans.

Denim gave blue a democratic mythology. What began as durable work clothing became a symbol of labor, rebellion, youth, and casual freedom. At the same time, darker blues became associated with authority, trust, and professionalism. Banks, governments, technology companies, and international organizations adopted blue because it suggested stability without the aggression of red or the severity of black.

Today blue carries many meanings at once. It can be sacred or corporate, melancholic or peaceful, aristocratic or ordinary. We speak of “feeling blue,” but also of blue skies and clear water. It is the color of distance, depth, uniforms, hyperlinks, passports, planets, and dreams.

The history of blue is therefore a history of rarity becoming abundance. Once costly, mysterious, and difficult to produce, blue is now one of the most common and beloved colors in the world. Its journey runs from Egyptian tombs and Afghan mines to medieval altarpieces, colonial plantations, factory dyes, denim jackets, and digital screens — a color that began as a precious substance and became a global language.
